title: States and Cities Sue to Block Trump Rule Linking Green Cards to Public Benefits
excerpt: Twenty-two states, D.C., and a six-government city coalition filed twin lawsuits Monday seeking to stop a Sept. 18 DHS rule that would let immigration officers deny green cards over use of Medicaid, food stamps, and even school meals.
body:
• Two lawsuits filed Monday in Manhattan federal court challenge the DHS "public charge" rule, which is scheduled to take effect on Friday, Sept. 18.
  • New York Attorney General Letitia James leads a coalition of 22 states plus the District of Columbia; New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani leads six local governments — New York City, Chicago, San Francisco, Santa Clara County, Seattle, and King County — in a parallel suit.
  • The rule would let immigration officers weigh non-cash benefits such as Medicaid and SNAP — and even benefits legally used by an applicant's family members — against green-card applicants, with no clear limits on what counts.
  • The states call the rule "arbitrary and capricious" and warn that billions in federal funding are at risk as eligible families drop benefits out of fear.

What happened

Dozens of Democratic-led states, counties, and cities sued the Trump administration on Monday to block a new federal rule that would allow immigration officials to deny green cards to people who use public benefits such as food stamps and Medicaid.

The two lawsuits were filed in Manhattan federal court the same day, Reuters reported. New York State Attorney General Letitia James, leading a coalition of 22 states plus the District of Columbia, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, leading a coalition of six local governments, announced the legal action at a City Hall news conference in Manhattan. Both seek to stop a Department of Homeland Security rule set to take effect on Friday.

"The rule would allow immigration officers to consider use of critical benefits like Medicaid and SNAP, and even participation in school meal programs, as part of an applicant's circumstance," James said at the briefing. "That means immigrant New Yorkers may be forced to ask themselves impossible questions: 'Will getting health insurance hurt my chances of getting a green card? Will accepting food assistance when I fall on hard times be held against me?'"

Context and background

At issue is the "public charge" provision of U.S. immigration law, which has long allowed the government to deny a visa or green card to someone deemed likely to become primarily dependent on government assistance. Under the Biden-era rule adopted in 2022, officials could consider an immigrant's receipt of cash aid such as supplemental security income, but not non-cash benefits like food stamps or Medicaid.

The rule announced by DHS in July revives a broader 2019 Trump-era policy: non-cash benefits can count against applicants, and officers may even consider benefits legally used by family members the applicant must support — including U.S. citizens. Per the Vermont attorney general's office, there is no clear limit on which benefits count, leaving families to guess what might endanger their status.

"Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported."

— Letitia James, New York State Attorney General

Impact and analysis

The plaintiffs argue the rule's real power is fear. California, Colorado, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico, and Wisconsin are among the states in the challenge; they contend mixed-status families will drop programs they are legally entitled to use, costing states billions in federal funding and driving up disease, medical costs, and poverty: forgoing legal access to benefits harms "public health, local economies, public education, and public safety," the filing argues.

Mamdani said the rule would have a "chilling effect" not only on immigrants seeking legal status but on other residents of the nation's largest city: "It is simply a vehicle for confusion and a vehicle for cruelty." A DHS spokesman, Chandler Rebel, dismissed the suits, telling USA Today that sanctuary states feared losing federal funds because immigrants "might remove themselves from American welfare programs" — adding, "We're shaking in our boots over this supposedly terrible outcome." The department has not otherwise responded to the lawsuits.

The diaspora angle

The rule lands squarely on the immigrant communities the case is meant to protect — including Indian families navigating the long employment- and family-based green-card backlogs. Because officers may weigh benefits used by U.S. citizen relatives, even established mixed-status households could face new scrutiny when sponsoring a parent or spouse. For the many H-1B holders adjusting status after years in the queue, the prospect that a child's school meal or a parent's Medicaid enrollment might be held against them turns everyday family decisions into immigration risks.

What to watch next

The rule is set to take effect on Friday, Sept. 18, and courts could be asked for emergency relief this week — the key question is whether the plaintiffs win a stay before enforcement begins. Beyond that, the states want a federal judge to vacate the rule as unlawful, a fight that could take months.
nri_angle: The expanded public-charge rule could affect Indian families in the green-card backlog and mixed-status households, where even a U.S. citizen relative's legal use of benefits might be weighed against a sponsored parent or spouse.
author: Diaspora Desk
